reconciled_candidates.label: One-Hot Encoding
reconciled_candidates.description: One-hot encoding represents each word as a sparse vector with a 1 at the vocabulary index and zeros elsewhere, resulting in high-dimensional, inefficient representations.
coverage_criteria: Create a one-hot vector for a given word from a small vocabulary.
Explain why one-hot vectors are sparse and high-dimensional.

reconciled_candidates.label: Count-Based Text Representations and Limitations
reconciled_candidates.description: Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF represent text by counting words (or n-grams) and weighting them by importance. Preprocessing steps like stemming and stop-word removal are common. These methods yield sparse vectors that ignore word context and cannot handle unknown words.
coverage_criteria: Compute Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF vectors for a small corpus.
List at least two limitations of count-based representations.
Explain the purpose of stemming and stop-word removal in text preprocessing.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates together describe count-based methods (BoW, TF-IDF), necessary preprocessing, and their shortcomings, forming a coherent unit that transitions into the need for dense embeddings.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly covers Bag-of-Words, N-gram, and TF-IDF as count-based techniques, with on-screen formulas and examples.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Grouping these three together as 'count-based methods' creates a teachable block that contrasts with later embedding approaches; it is checkable with a few computation tasks.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video enumerates these three shortcomings explicitly as motivation for embeddings.

reconciled_candidates.label: Word Embeddings as Dense Vectors
reconciled_candidates.description: Unlike sparse encodings, word embeddings are dense numerical vectors where each dimension captures latent features. They are lower-dimensional than the vocabulary and enable models to process semantic meaning efficiently.
coverage_criteria: Define word embeddings and contrast them with sparse representations.
Explain why dense vectors are more efficient than one-hot vectors.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates introduce embeddings: one gives the general definition, the other focuses on density. Together they provide a complete introductory concept.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video introduces word embeddings as mathematical representations of text necessary for ML models.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational definition that sets the stage for all subsequent topics; it is narrow enough to be checked with a single recall question.

source_metadata.source_name: A Complete Overview of Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video defines a dense vector and contrasts it with sparse representations right after introducing embeddings.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This specific property of embeddings is a core checkable fact that supports understanding of embedding efficiency.

reconciled_candidates.label: Semantic Similarity and Properties of Embedding Space
reconciled_candidates.description: In a distributional framework, words are similar if they share similar contexts. Embedding vectors place these words in a space where distance (e.g., cosine) reflects similarity. Well‑trained embeddings also exhibit clustering of related words and support analogical reasoning (e.g., king - man + woman ≈ queen).
coverage_criteria: Explain how word similarity is defined by context rather than spelling.
Given a 2D plot, identify which words are most similar based on distance.
Describe the analogy property of ideal embeddings with an example.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These three candidates build a narrative from contextual similarity to distance‑based similarity and finally the desired properties of clustering and analogies, making a cohesive teachable segment.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video uses the 'tea/coffee' vs 'tea/pea' example to illustrate distributional similarity.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept is small enough to check by asking for a definition and an original example.

reconciled_candidates.description: A neural network can include an embedding layer initialized randomly and trained end‑to‑end for a specific task, producing specialized word representations. This requires large amounts of data.

State one advantage and one disadvantage of training embeddings from scratch.

reconciled_candidates.label: Word2vec: CBOW and Skip‑gram Architectures
reconciled_candidates.description: Word2vec learns embeddings by training a shallow neural network on a prediction task: Continuous Bag‑of‑Words (CBOW) predicts a target word from context, while Skip‑gram predicts context words from a target word.
coverage_criteria: Differentiate CBOW and Skip‑gram and state what each predicts.
Explain how Word2vec creates dense word vectors from unlabeled text.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate describes both architectures and forms a single well‑defined technique.

reconciled_candidates.label: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
reconciled_candidates.description: GloVe improves on Word2vec by leveraging a word co‑occurrence matrix, training vectors such that their dot product approximates the log of co‑occurrence probability, thereby incorporating global corpus statistics.
coverage_criteria: Explain how GloVe differs from Word2vec regarding global information.
Describe the role of the co‑occurrence matrix in GloVe.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate specifically addresses GloVe and its unique mechanism; no other candidates cover it.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video states GloVe adds global context to Word2vec and shows the co-occurrence matrix and training equation.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific enhancement of Word2vec, checkable by asking for the key difference.

reconciled_candidates.label: fastText: Subword Embeddings
reconciled_candidates.description: fastText represents each word as the sum of its character n‑gram embeddings, allowing it to build vectors for out‑of‑vocabulary words and handle morphologically rich languages.
coverage_criteria: Explain how fastText’s subword approach addresses the out‑of‑vocabulary problem.
Describe the difference between Word2vec and fastText regarding word representation.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate fully covers the fastText method and its benefits.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video describes fastText's subword training with an example and highlights its benefits for rare words.

reconciled_candidates.label: ELMo: Contextualized Word Embeddings
reconciled_candidates.description: ELMo uses a bidirectional LSTM to produce word vectors that depend on the entire input sentence, allowing the same word to have different representations in different contexts (e.g., homonyms).
coverage_criteria: Explain why ELMo provides different embeddings for the same word in different sentences.
Describe the advantage of context‑dependent over static word embeddings.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate is the only one covering ELMo and stands alone.

reconciled_candidates.label: Using Pre‑trained Word Embeddings
reconciled_candidates.description: Pre‑trained word vectors can be used in two ways: as static features (fixed during downstream training) or fine‑tuned (adjusted to the task). The Gensim library provides convenient access to pre‑trained models (Word2vec, GloVe, fastText) and similarity operations.

Write code to load a pre‑trained model from Gensim and find similar words.

reconciled_candidates.label: TF-IDF Definition and Computation
reconciled_candidates.description: TF-IDF is a statistical measure of word relevance in a document corpus, computed as the product of Term Frequency (TF) and Inverse Document Frequency (IDF). TF measures how often a term appears in a document, normalized by document length. IDF measures how rare a term is across the corpus, using log(N/df). The product gives a weight that highlights terms that are frequent in a specific document but rare overall, yielding document feature vectors.
coverage_criteria: Define TF-IDF and its purpose.
Calculate TF, IDF, and TF-IDF for a given term in a small corpus.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All candidates describe the same core idea: the definition, components, and arithmetic of TF-IDF.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video introduces TF-IDF as a popular text representation, defines it as the product of TF and IDF, and summarizes its purpose and applications.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept encapsulates the core idea of TF-IDF and is checkable with basic recall questions, while allowing deeper understanding to be assessed by elaborating on its components.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly defines TF and walks through a worked example calculating TF('fox', d1)=2/12 and TF('fox', d2)=3/12.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: TF is a fundamental building block of TF-IDF and is small enough to be verified with a simple arithmetic exercise.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video defines IDF and provides the formula log(N/df), then calculates IDF('fox', D)=log(2/2)=0, illustrating that a term in all documents gets zero IDF.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: IDF is a key concept that can be checked by asking the student to compute it for a simple corpus or interpret the result.

extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a key concept of the chapter, teachable as a single formula with components.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The text provides the tf-idf formula and explains each part: tf is frequency divided by document length; idf uses log and document counts.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Understanding the formula is crucial for deeper use of TF-IDF.

reconciled_candidates.label: TF-IDF Output: Document Vectors and Applications
reconciled_candidates.description: After computing TF-IDF for all terms, each document is represented as a weighted term vector, where high weights indicate discriminative terms. These document vectors are used in data mining tasks such as classification, clustering, and information retrieval, especially document search.
coverage_criteria: Explain how TF-IDF transforms documents into feature vectors.
List at least three applications of TF-IDF in text analysis.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All candidates cover the output representation and practical uses of TF-IDF.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly states that each document becomes a feature vector and the corpus is a set of these feature vectors, which can be used in classification, clustering, or retrieval.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept bridges TF-IDF calculation to practical applications, and it can be verified by asking the student to explain the transformation or list tasks.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video summarizes that TF-IDF has many uses, most importantly in automated text analysis, and is very useful for scoring words in ML algorithms for NLP, and was invented for document search and information retrieval.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This provides a high-level perspective on the value of TF-IDF and can be checked with recall of the applications mentioned in the source.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source mentions that words repeating less have 'maior importância' (higher importance), indicating that TF-IDF highlights significant terms.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Understanding output interpretation is essential for using TF-IDF effectively.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The text describes that TF-IDF provides a vector of characteristics for each document, and shows the resulting matrix.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational concept for text representation in NLP.

reconciled_candidates.label: TF-IDF Discriminative Power and Comparison with Bag of Words
reconciled_candidates.description: TF-IDF assigns higher weights to terms that appear frequently in a specific document but rarely across the corpus, making them discriminative features. A term that appears in every document gets IDF=0 and thus TF-IDF=0, meaning it has no discriminative power. This contrasts with Bag of Words, which merely counts occurrences and does not differentiate important terms from common ones.
coverage_criteria: Explain why a word with IDF=0 is not useful for distinguishing documents.
Describe the key difference between Bag of Words and TF-IDF.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates address the weighting behavior of TF-IDF and its advantage over simple counts, covering the special case of zero IDF.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The example calculates IDF('fox') = log(2/2) = 0, leading to TF-IDF = 0, and concludes that 'fox' is equally (equivalently zero) relevant to both documents, illustrating that such a term lacks discriminative power.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This insight reveals the intuitive justification for IDF and can be assessed with a single interpretation question.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The text explicitly contrasts bag of words and TF-IDF, noting BOW's problem of highlighting frequent but irrelevant words, and TF-IDF's ability to adjust for term frequency across documents.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Understanding the distinction is crucial for choosing the right text representation method.

reconciled_candidates.label: Implementing TF-IDF with Scikit-learn: TfidfVectorizer and Preprocessing
reconciled_candidates.description: In Python, TF-IDF can be computed using TfidfVectorizer from sklearn. This requires preparing text by splitting into documents (e.g., splitlines) and optionally removing stopwords using NLTK's stopwords list, passed to the stop_words parameter. The fit_transform method returns a TF-IDF matrix.
coverage_criteria: Write code to import TfidfVectorizer, include stopwords from NLTK, and fit_transform a list of documents.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All candidates describe practical steps for implementing TF-IDF in Python with scikit-learn: using the vectorizer, stopword removal, and document splitting.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The text provides an example using TfidfVectorizer, showing parameters and usage with Wikipedia data and stopwords.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical skill for applying TF-IDF in Python.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The example code uses stopwords from nltk to remove articles, prepositions, etc., improving TF-IDF results.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Stopword removal is a key preprocessing step that can be taught independently but is closely tied to TF-IDF implementation.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The code example uses splitlines() to split the Wikipedia page into paragraphs before feeding to TfidfVectorizer.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical step in preparing data for TF-IDF analysis.

reconciled_candidates.label: NLP Vocabulary: Document, Body, Dictionary, Topic
reconciled_candidates.description: In NLP, a document is a single data instance (e.g., a paragraph, tweet). The body (or corpus) is the collection of all documents. The dictionary is the set of all unique words occurring in at least one document. A topic is a collection of co-occurring words that represent a theme.
coverage_criteria: Define the terms document, body (corpus), dictionary, and topic in NLP.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate introduces the fundamental NLP vocabulary needed for understanding text representation methods.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly defines these terms at the start to establish a common vocabulary for understanding LSA.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: These four terms are fundamental and small enough to be checked together in a single question asking for definitions.

reconciled_candidates.label: Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) Definition
reconciled_candidates.description: LSA is an unsupervised NLP technique that discovers latent topics in a corpus by applying dimensionality reduction (via SVD) to the document-term matrix, yielding lower-dimensional encodings of documents as combinations of topics.
coverage_criteria: Explain what LSA is and its purpose in text analysis.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate provides the core definition of LSA.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The section 'Understanding Latent Semantic Analysis' introduces LSA as an unsupervised technique targeting latent features and dimensionality reduction.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept captures the core definition of LSA in one teachable idea, appropriate for a single check-in question.

reconciled_candidates.label: Document-Term Matrix in LSA
reconciled_candidates.description: A document-term matrix is a representation where rows correspond to documents, columns to dictionary words, and cells indicate word presence or frequency. It serves as the input to SVD in LSA.
coverage_criteria: Describe the structure of a document-term matrix.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate explains the matrix representation that LSA builds upon.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explains the document-term matrix in detail, showing an example with four sentence fragments and binary values.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Focusing on the document-term matrix as a standalone concept allows checking understanding of this key representation method.

reconciled_candidates.label: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) in LSA
reconciled_candidates.description: In LSA, Singular Value Decomposition is applied to the document-term matrix to reduce its dimensionality and extract latent topics, analogous to PCA. This transforms the high-dimensional word space into a lower-dimensional topic space.
coverage_criteria: State the role of SVD in LSA and its analogy to PCA.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate focuses on the SVD step that gives LSA its latent topic discovery capability.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video dedicates a section to SVD, explaining it as the second step of LSA that reduces dimensionality and encodes data with latent topics.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept isolates SVD's role in LSA, making it checkable with a question about its purpose and analogy to PCA.

lesson.title: Outras técnicas Word Embedding: TF, TF-IDF e LSA
lesson.description: Ao longo deste encontro, outras técnicas de Word Embedding serão apresentadas as pessoas desenvolvedoras. Assim, o objetivo desta abordagem é que elas possam comparar as técnicas que foram apresentadas e verificar que cada uma delas possui um tipo de aplicação característica para sua aplicação.
